title: John Nay — Norm Ai / Norm Law (founder interview)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Nay supports the narrower claim that legal AI requires domain-expert supervision, quality assurance and client-specific context. However, he does not address whether automation erodes junior apprenticeship, creates an expertise-reproduction paradox or requires reconstructed associate training, so his position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: And on the starting point, I mean even that uh it still takes a lot of domain expertise uh not necessarily to write code anymore, but to supervise what's coming out of what you're writing code for and to make sure that there's a sort of a quality assurance and trust layer of having attorneys and domain experts, ex-regulators, etc.

And and that that's one thing and then the second thing is around uh how do you have a process and  a technology to tailor that base AI agent to a given client's context and then work super closely with the client to keep that updated and and have that be sort of a living breathing AI agent that understands uh the specifics and the nuances of of their firm.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks

His claims support bounded, maintained agents rather than unattended autonomous legal practice, though he provides no measured reliability or savings evidence.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Nay accepts the cluster’s core augmentation model: AI should handle scalable processes while scarce human time shifts toward higher-order judgment. He materially extends it by arguing that, once usefulness is credibly validated, legal and compliance departments may bear an emerging obligation to justify non-adoption.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Nay accepts the cluster’s core work-redesign proposition: AI should absorb suitable processes so scarce human time shifts toward higher-order judgment. He materially extends the operating-model analysis with build-versus-buy criteria, including internal context, maintenance, industry knowledge, trust and external risk assumption. His broad adoption presumption is less task-specific and empirically supported than the cluster’s selective-deployment framing, but does not displace it.
qs: So, those are all factors of of why you would still make a decision to work with someone outside of your company instead of just building it yourself.

kp.k: Combined technology and legal services offer clients delivery choices
kp.d: Nay describes Norm AI as a legal and compliance technology company that also powers Norm Law, which he calls the first AI-native law firm built for institutional clients. He presents the combination as allowing asset managers and financial institutions to choose between outside legal services and technology for their in-house teams, using shared client data and team expertise. The claimed market first is his characterization, not a documented comparative finding.
qs: So, Norm AI is a is a technology company focused on legal and compliance AI, but we also power Norm Law.
So, Norm Law is the first AI native law firm really built for institutional clients.
Is it best to do this through an outside counsel type function, or is it best to in-house some of this for your in-house team to use as your own technology?

kp.k: Text, structure and precedent make law amenable to AI
kp.d: Nay attributes language models' suitability for legal work to text-based training, structured legal reasoning analogous to code, and law's reliance on precedent. He reports a major capability increase with large language models and recalls exploratory Stanford Codex research on understanding fiduciary duties three or four years earlier. These are qualitative observations; he supplies no benchmark results or study design.
qs: the fact that there's so much text and the fact that language models are trained on text in an unsupervised way at first, that is a great starting point for why it's good at that.
And it's it's very amenable to to a process that's almost similar to code in a way.
I had been doing some sort of research on the side at at Stanford Codex around how well these models can understand things like fiduciary duties.
it was still early and this is, you know, three or four years ago.

kp.k: Specialized agents require expert supervision and continuing client tailoring
kp.d: Nay describes two requirements for legal and regulatory agents: domain expertise in developing and supervising a workflow-specific starting point, and ongoing tailoring to each client's context. Attorneys, domain experts and former regulators provide quality assurance and trust, while close client collaboration keeps the agent current. Easier coding therefore does not eliminate expert involvement in checking outputs.
qs: building a specialized domain-specific AI agent for a given workflow in legal and regulatory.
it still takes a lot of domain expertise uh not necessarily to write code anymore, but to supervise what's coming out of what you're writing code for
a sort of a quality assurance and trust layer of having attorneys and domain experts, ex-regulators, etc. uh super involved in the process.

kp.k: Easier coding shifts the rationale for buying external services
kp.d: Nay argues that internal teams increasingly can build suitable tools because code is easier to write and they possess superior company context. He locates external providers' continuing value in maintenance, industry-wide learning and market norms, and a trusted party's willingness to take responsibility for correctness. He raises offloading liability as a purchasing consideration, without describing contractual arrangements or establishing that liability actually transfers.
qs: the build versus buy it's changing very quickly because it's just so much easier to write code.
The question then becomes maintaining that.
It also becomes tapping into the broader industry context and other learnings from other companies in an efficient way.
is there is there a way to have sort of the the liability or the trust layer be offloaded to someone else?
a party that you can sort of trust to be the ones that are in charge of this and that are taking on the risk of saying we're doing this correctly.

kp.k: AI-native workflows put agents first and humans in supervision
kp.d: Nay characterizes innovative organizations as reorganizing workflows around agents performing the first pass, rather than merely assisting a human-led process. Humans remain supervisors and complementary professionals, so his pilot metaphor does not describe unsupervised reliance on AI. He argues that this arrangement reveals AI's strengths and weaknesses and enables iterative improvements for subsequent similar tasks; no measured productivity or quality gains are provided.
qs: you reorient a workflow around an AI agent or set of them doing the first pass of the task.

instead of having a human be the the pilot and then you have a co-pilot AI, you kind of flip it and you have the AI be the pilot in a way and have have humans be co-pilots and supervisors and complementing
really figure out where is the AI good and where is it not good
then they can make a change and then it goes back and improves marginally at least for the next time that something similar is done

kp.k: Failure to adopt useful AI may become a risk
kp.d: Nay suggests an approaching inflection point at which declining demonstrably helpful AI could itself become problematic for legal and compliance risk management. His argument is conditional on usefulness and validation; he asserts that his company demonstrates empirical value but supplies no supporting measurements here. This is an adoption argument, not a statement of an established professional or regulatory duty.
qs: I think it it's getting to a point where AI is so good that if you're not using AI to reduce regulatory and legal risk and to supervise your operations and other things that nature then that's actually becoming the problem.
especially if it's provided by someone who's really good at validating it like we are in showing that it empirically is really helpful, then that's kind of a problem, maybe.
Well, why am I not going to use something that's actually going to improve uh the legal and compliance department?

kp.k: Automation should reserve scarce human time for higher-order judgment
kp.d: Nay invokes decades of technology use in legal and compliance as a precedent for reallocating human work when technology performs tasks better. He frames AI adoption as freeing finite professional hours for higher-order judgment, contrasting human time constraints with AI's capacity to run parallel processes. He does not quantify staffing changes or specify effects on particular lawyer seniority levels.
qs: People have been using technology in legal and compliance for for many decades now
then humans moved up the the stack and did higher-order work that was a better use of their judgment.
it's actually just trying to better allocate the scarce hours that we have as as as biological entities, right?
can't clone ourselves like AIs can and  run a million background processes.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: John Nay claims that combining a legal-AI technology business with an AI-native law firm enables client-specific choices between outside legal services and in-house technology.
pts.d: Nay distinguishes Norm AI, the technology company, from Norm Law, the legal-services provider it powers. He describes Norm Law as the first AI-native law firm built for institutional clients and claims that combining technology, client data and a professional team enables better service. The proposed advantage is flexibility over whether work is delivered through outside counsel or brought into the client's own team using technology. The priority claim about being the first is Nay's characterization.

pts.k: Nay claims that large language models have substantially improved at legal reasoning and that law's textual, structured and precedent-driven character helps explain their suitability.
pts.d: He links legal capability to models' training on text, analogizes structured legal reasoning to coding, and identifies historical precedent as a helpful starting point. He reports that the transition from language models to large language models produced a major capability increase, including in understanding fiduciary duties. These are qualitative capability claims, not reported benchmark results.

pts.k: Nay claims that legal and regulatory agents require expert supervision, client tailoring and continuing updates, even as writing code becomes easier.
pts.d: He describes two layers of development: a workflow-specific base agent built with attorneys, domain experts and former regulators involved in quality assurance; and a client-specific adaptation maintained through close collaboration. Expertise shifts away from necessarily writing code toward supervising outputs and supplying a quality-assurance and trust layer. His model retains human verification rather than relying on unreviewed AI output.

pts.k: Nay claims that easier coding changes build-versus-buy decisions, shifting external providers' value toward maintenance, industry knowledge, trust and risk-bearing.
pts.d: Internal teams have an advantage in knowing their own company's context and can increasingly build tailored software. Nay nevertheless identifies reasons to retain an outside provider: maintaining systems, accessing learning across companies, understanding market norms and having another party take responsibility for doing the work correctly. His discussion of offloading liability is a proposed value driver, not a description of a specific contractual transfer of liability.

pts.k: Nay claims that innovative organizations are making AI the first-pass operator and humans the supervisors, with repeated use enabling incremental improvement.
pts.d: He contrasts a human-led workflow assisted by an AI copilot with an AI-native workflow organized around agents performing the first pass. Humans remain involved as supervisors and complements; the claim is not one of fully unsupervised legal-service substitution. Nay argues that this arrangement reveals capability boundaries and lets professionals extend them through changes that improve subsequent similar work. He does not specify whether those changes involve model training, configuration or workflow redesign.

pts.k: Nay predicts an emerging inflection point at which failing to use demonstrably helpful AI becomes the problem, while humans concentrate on higher-order judgment.
pts.d: He argues that AI is becoming sufficiently useful for legal processes, compliance and operational supervision that organizations should increasingly justify non-use. The argument is conditional on knowing that a tool is helpful and on validation by a capable provider. He presents this tentatively, rather than identifying an established legal duty to adopt AI. Drawing on earlier technology adoption, he anticipates reallocating scarce human time toward work requiring judgment rather than making an explicit headcount or employment forecast.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest principally on Nay's research experience, descriptions of his businesses, qualitative observations and analogies; the interview supplies no quantitative findings.
pts.d: Nay invokes approximately 13 years studying language models' understanding of law and policy, an AI research background and PhD, and work at Stanford Codex on fiduciary duties. He uses the analogy between law and coding to explain suitability and prior legal-technology adoption to support the shift toward higher-order human work. His account of Norm AI and Norm Law supplies an operating-model example. He asserts that his company validates usefulness empirically, but gives no methods, measurements, named client outcomes, comparative results or published studies. Statements about what innovative organizations are doing are not accompanied by named examples. The Stanford Codex reference is his account of his own research, not a cited Stanford RegLab hallucination study.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most claims describe present changes or an approaching inflection point at the interview's stated 2026 date, with no precise future adoption deadline.
pts.d: Nay places early observations of fiduciary-duty understanding three or four years before the interview and contrasts them with current capabilities. He describes build-versus-buy changes as happening very quickly and AI-first workflows as already used by innovative organizations. Effective deployment depends on domain-specific workflows, professional supervision, client tailoring, ongoing maintenance and updates. His argument against non-adoption depends on demonstrated usefulness and validation, not simply the availability of any AI system. The interview gives no timetable for profession-wide restructuring or complete automation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are institutional legal-services buyers, their internal legal and compliance teams, outside providers and expert professionals.
pts.d: Asset managers and financial institutions are the named client segments. Their in-house teams gain options to build or use technology internally rather than procure all work as outside legal services. Legal and compliance departments and operational supervisors are the intended beneficiaries of risk reduction and improved allocation of human time. Outside counsel and technology providers face a value proposition centered on expertise, maintenance, client context, trust and responsibility. Attorneys, domain specialists and former regulators contribute supervision and quality assurance, while professionals increasingly provide judgment around AI first-pass work. Nay does not extend these claims to consumer access to justice, specific associate staffing structures, pricing changes or quantified job losses.
